South Korea Stock Market Crash: KOSPI plunges over 8% amid tech sell-off; Samsung, SK Hynix tumble
sum: South Korea Stock Market Crash: South Korea's benchmark stock index, the KOSPI, plunged over 8 per cent on Thursday, November 5, triggering a circuit breaker as heavyweight stocks Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix tumbled amid a sharp sell-off in global technology stocks.

As of 6:10 am, the KOSPI was trading 6.5 per cent lower, down 364.24 points at 5,019.56. Earlier in the session, the index had slumped to an intraday low of 4,911.28, marking a decline of 8.8 per cent from the previous close of 5,383.80.
The sharp decline in South Korea's stock market came amid concerns over AI data-centre investments, a sell-off in US semiconductor stocks and weakness in the country's major chipmakers.

AI data-centre concerns: Investors are concerned that the Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections could lead to tighter regulations on data centres and power consumption. This could delay new AI infrastructure projects and reduce future demand for chips.

US semiconductor sell-off: The decline in US chip stocks spilled over into South Korea's export- and semiconductor-heavy market. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) slipped around 10 per cent, marking its worst performance since March 2020.
Samsung and SK Hynix weakness: Shares of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, two of the KOSPI's heavyweight constituents, led the decline.

Samsung Electronics shares were trading around 7 per cent lower at 1,87,200. The stock had touched an intraday low of 1,79,200, reflecting a decline of over 11 per cent from its previous close of 2,01,500.

After SK Hynix's 57% Plunge, iM Securities Says HBM Alone Justifies Market Cap, Sets Target at approximately $1,700
sum: With SK Hynix (000660) shares having fallen by more than half from their June peak, iM Securities has set a target price of 2.3 million won (approximately $1,700), citing the value of the company's high-bandwidth memory (HBM) business. That implies 64.5% upside from the closing price of 1.398 million won (approximately $1,000) on the 29th of last month.

iM Securities issued a Buy rating on SK Hynix in a report on the 4th. The core argument is that the current share price has excessively priced in concerns about an earnings collapse after 2028. Ko Eui-young, an analyst at iM Securities, noted that "the stock has fallen 57% from its June 2026 high to its October low, exceeding the 51% average decline of past downturns," and that "a correction that previously took 8 to 13 months has played out in just four months this time." The diagnosis is that the market is assuming an earnings cliff in 2028.

The report's centerpiece is a revaluation of the HBM business. iM Securities estimates that SK Hynix's HBM revenue will grow from 43 trillion won (approximately $32.0 billion) in 2026 to 183 trillion won (approximately $136.2 billion) in 2028. Applying TSMC's price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio for each period to the HBM business's after-tax profit yields a business value of about 946 trillion won (approximately $704.0 billion) in 2027, equivalent to 93% of the current market capitalization. By 2028, that rises to about 1,372 trillion won (approximately $1.0 trillion), or 135% of market capitalization.

Note: 2026 revenue is the annual forecast presented in the report; 2027 revenue was not separately provided. Business value shares are based on market capitalization at the time the report was written.

Ko emphasized that "this means that by 2027, HBM alone already explains the current market capitalization," adding that "even targeting a multiple of 10x, which the market typically accepts, the result is not much different."

The earnings outlook is also on an upward trajectory. iM Securities estimates SK Hynix's consolidated revenue this year at 364.37 trillion won (approximately $271.2 billion) and operating profit at 283.745 trillion won (approximately $211.2 billion).

sum: Kioxia's cautious December-quarter forecast rattled memory stocks and raised a question the entire sector is now wrestling with: does soft guidance from Japan's largest chipmaker signal a cooling AI memory cycle, or is the selloff noise ahead of a March…

A cautious forecast from Kioxia Holdings, Japan’s largest memory chipmaker, turned an overnight gain in Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU | MU Price Prediction) into a loss and pulled memory stocks lower. Micron stock is at $853.34, down 4% this afternoon. The decline adds to a pullback from an AI-fueled run in the chipmaker’s shares.

Over the past month, Micron stock is down 20%. That slide comes despite record results: on September 30, the company reported Q4 FY2026 revenue of $54.23 billion, up 379.3% year over year, with an adjusted gross margin of 87%. For Q1 FY2027, Micron forecast its revenue to $61.5 billion, plus or minus $1.5 billion.

Kioxia Holdings guided its December-quarter operating profit to 2 trillion yen, the company said on November 2. That forecast stands only slightly above the 1.99 trillion yen Kioxia earned in the September quarter, and it came in below analyst estimates. Shares of Kioxia declined in Tokyo as investors digested the outlook.

The company attributed the soft outlook mainly to shipment timing, saying some orders were pulled into the September quarter while others were pushed into the March quarter. Chief Financial Officer Yoshihiko Kawamura said Kioxia expects a return to rapid growth in the March quarter. He added that AI data center demand remains robust and that Kioxia has sold out its planned output for next year.

Micron’s slide also follows a weak prior session on October 30, when Samsung missed profit expectations. The open question for the group is whether Kioxia’s outlook signals cooling AI memory demand and pricing, or whether the selling reflects broader tech positioning.

Western Digital (NASDAQ:WDC) stock is at $347.24, down 5%. That’s a steeper decline than Micron’s, making the hard drive maker the weakest of the three. During the past month, Western Digital has lost 24%. The company sells to hyperscalers, cloud service providers and enterprises building out storage for the AI-driven data economy.

sum: Driven by Anthropic's push for an initial public offering (IPO) and SK hynix's expanded shareholder returns, SK hynix rose 11.04% and SK Square climbed 15.74% during the final week of October (the 26th–30). However, concerns over the sustainability of AI investment resurfaced following earnings reports from major U.S. tech companies, suggesting that volatility in semiconductor stocks is likely to persist for the time being.

According to Korea Exchange data on the 31st, the KOSPI closed at 5,730.74 this week, up 180.44 points (3.25%) from Jeonju (5,550.30). On the 26th (local time), news that Anthropic was pursuing an IPO eased concerns about AI profitability. Additionally, semiconductor stocks surged after SK hynix announced third-quarter results exceeding market expectations and plans to expand shareholder returns on the 28th. However, doubts about the sustainability and profitability of AI investment grew again following consecutive earnings releases from Alphabet, Intel, and Amazon, causing semiconductor stocks to plunge sharply on the 30th.

As a result, SK hynix and Samsung Electronics posted gains of only 11.04% and 4.41%, respectively, from the 26th to the 30th. In the case of Samsung Electronics, the rise was smaller than that of SK hynix because the expected shareholder return policy was not announced. Since SK hynix announced an expansion of shareholder returns, SK Square, which holds shares in the company, also jumped 15.74%.

Nevertheless, with concerns over AI profitability rising again, volatility in semiconductor stocks appears unavoidable. Researcher Cho A-in at Samsung Securities stated, "We expect domestic stock markets to remain highly volatile for the time being, driven by changes in the earnings and outlooks of AI companies, macroeconomic conditions, and supply and demand dynamics." She added, "In particular, whether the correction on the 30th will be limited to a temporary dip in investor sentiment or lead to downward revisions in profit forecasts for AI-related companies will be a key variable determining the future direction of the market."
Beyond semiconductors, stocks that posted third-quarter results exceeding expectations also saw significant gains.

sum: - SK Hynix is reportedly considering the special dividend after booking an estimated 20 trillion won in gains from trimming its Kioxia stake.
- The chipmaker scrapped plans for a U.S. IPO of its Solidigm subsidiary.

SK Hynix (SKHY) is considering a special dividend of 16 trillion won ($12 billion), funded by gains from its investment in Japanese memory-chip maker Kioxia Holdings, South Korea's Dong-A Ilbo reported Monday, citing unnamed investment banking sources.

The payout would amount to about 80% of an estimated 20 trillion won in gains SK Hynix booked from its Kioxia investment in the first half of 2026. The company is expected to announce its plans alongside third-quarter earnings on Wednesday, according to the report.
SK Hynix's Seoul-listed shares rose marginally in Asian trading hours on Monday morning, while the U.S.-listed stock was up over 1% in overnight trading late Sunday.

SK Hynix said it was reviewing options to return money to shareholders but had not decided on a special dividend, according to a Bloomberg report, which added that the prospect of a payout has helped the stock hold up amid a broader selloff in AI-related shares.
SK Hynix joined a Bain Capital-led consortium in 2018 to acquire Toshiba's former memory-chip business for $18 billion. Kioxia's value climbed following its Tokyo stock-market debut in 2024.

Josh Gilbert, APAC lead analyst at investment platform eToro, said the rebound indicated that shareholders had welcomed the decision to keep Solidigm within the group.

Samsung shares fell 3.6% to 252,500 won, while SK Hynix dropped 3.4% to 1,624,000 won. CXMT shares also declined 3.1% to 49.42 yuan.

CXMT said it had made key progress on a so-called 4F² memory-cell structure that is also being pursued by Samsung and SK Hynix. The technology is designed to fit more memory cells onto a chip, potentially increasing storage capacity while improving efficiency.

Mainstream commercial dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) currently uses a 6F² cell structure. CXMT's approach relies on a proprietary Vertical Surrounding Gate transistor, which uses a vertical gate architecture to reduce current leakage while shrinking the area occupied by each memory cell, according to the South China Morning Post.

CXMT President Cao Kanyu said at an industry event in Shanghai over the weekend that the company planned to introduce a new generation of DDR5 registered dual in-line memory modules (RDIMMs) based on the technology by the end of 2026.
The modules are designed for enterprise servers, where memory products must meet demanding requirements for reliability, endurance and compatibility.

CXMT did not disclose detailed technical specifications or a specific launch date for the new product. The commercial impact of its latest development will therefore depend on its ability to bring the technology to market and meet the requirements of server customers.

Memory stocks are leading an AI-infrastructure selloff early Monday. Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU | MU Price Prediction) stock is down 6% to $916.03, SanDisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) stock is falling 6% to $1,531, and SK Hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY) stock is declining 7% to $175.98.

The move follows weekend commentary from the chief executives of Anthropic and OpenAI calling for a deliberate slowdown in the pace of AI capability advancement. Memory names carry some of the richest AI-infrastructure expectations in the market, which is why the reaction is concentrated inside the group rather than spread evenly across large-cap technology.

The Roundhill Memory ETF (CBOE:DRAM) is down 7%, while the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is down 2%. The memory fund is falling several times as hard as the broader NASDAQ 100, which places the selling inside the memory complex rather than across the market.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay on Saturday stating, “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he agreed, and posted early Monday that pacing does “not mean ‘stopping.'” Anthropic and OpenAI are privately held, and neither company has signaled a change to capital plans or model-training budgets.

Bernstein analyst Madison Rezaei framed the memory reaction directly, writing, “At this point, it’s not a call for a lowering of capex or stopping model training. However, many investors have started to question what happens if training slows.” That note captures why the selling in memory names is theme-level. The essays change sentiment immediately and change hyperscaler orders only if anyone acts on them.
SK Hynix is the most direct memory read on AI training demand, serving as the primary HBM supplier for NVIDIA AI accelerators, and its 7% drop is the deepest of the three names.

sum: KB Securities reports that Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix face severe memory supply shortages, with inventories dropping below 10 days amid surging AI infrastructure demand and HBM4 transition strains. DRAM and NAND demand will exceed supply by over 10% next year. Despite recent stock pullbacks of nearly 28% to 40% driven by market leverage concerns, both companies are severely undervalued with record earnings expected. Technically, SK Hynix ADR approaches its period high of $178.41, with strong upside momentum toward Fibonacci extensions at $185.73 and $195.04, while short-term support rests near $172.65.

TradingKey - South Korean brokerage KB Securities pointed out in its latest research report that memory semiconductor inventories at Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix (SKHY) have dropped to less than 10 days of supply, and available supply next year will be significantly insufficient.

The firm added that as artificial intelligence infrastructure investment expands at an unprecedented pace, the memory chip market is facing a severe supply shortage. A key factor exacerbating the supply shortage is the transition to next-generation High Bandwidth Memory HBM4.

The firm believes that HBM4 requires about three times as many wafers as traditional DRAM. Due to limited wafer capacity, the full-scale mass production of HBM4 will inevitably reduce available capacity for traditional DRAM. KB Securities expects that DRAM and NAND demand will consequently exceed supply by more than 10 percentage points next year.

KB Securities stated that despite the supply deficit in the memory market, stock prices of both Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix have pulled back significantly over the past period, with Samsung Electronics falling nearly 28% from its peak and SK Hynix dropping nearly 40%. The decline in stock prices for both companies is related to a broad pullback in memory stocks and excessive leverage in the South Korean stock market.

While the stock price declines reflect market concerns, analysts said the stocks of the two companies are severely undervalued relative to their fundamentals, with earnings expected to hit record highs for three consecutive years.
